title: Does my game looks like AI slop? its a butcher shop incremental
author: Fraanciscoo
selftext: So, it’s an incremental game focused on building up your own butcher shop. This is a screenshot from the very beginning of the game; the goal is for you to evolve the shop, discovering increasingly better—and stranger—ways to process meat and earn money. My concern, though, is that the aesthetic screams "Aislop."

comments.author: HouseOfWyrd
comments.body:
Level of detail is simply how many details are included in a piece of art. Usually, human designers will limit the level of detail based on how important that asset is or how up-close people look at it. This is a time and resource saving measure.

A machine doesn't really have this problem or the context, and so will stuff all art with a consistently high level of detail, rendering things that simply don't need to be there.

This isn't a terrible example of that, but it's just ever so slightly more detailed than you'd expect for the presentation.

Based on 1 screenshot I cannot see if it’s slop. The visuals look nice, I think there is some clues to the image that AI was used.

Just enjoy the process, play it, let others share their opinion. And who cares if it is slop then? If it sticks it’s a game. Many people enjoy endless pages of youtube shorts 😂

comments.author: featherless_fiend
comments.body:
One very common identifier I see in tons of vibe coded games is when the UI is filled with words words words. I've (manually) worked on UIs a lot and I don't think being wordy looks good. Besides hurting immersion, a lot of times the extra text feels unnecessary.

If you look at old Bullfrog games they always use little pictures to represent things, that was a golden age. So the other day I even put this in my agents.md file:

- Instead of writing text in the UI, always try to use images to represent stuff. Text is immersion breaking! Animate the UI images using various shader effects.

comments.author: Briskfall
comments.body:
To put it in simple terms:

The UI/menu/interface is toon: pastel-vintage palette and pixelated aesthetics (easy on the eyes) -- emulating a warm "lighting" close to "soft"

while the isometric gameplay shows: runescape-level of low poly models; charred/high level of contrast colour wise -- warm lighting close to "hot," jagged anti-aliasing that makes it not as sharp as the "pixel UI" floating above

When there are too many elements that clash, it becomes very perceptible and not "easy on the eye." The human brain can "sense" something off -- often those who don't have the vocabulary will use a shorthand "it looks bad/slop" and won't be able to give a targeted response as they haven't read about it. But they can still "sense something off" because it's *innate* to them at a certain level, just not having the vocabulary.

This is less of a "game design" issue that plagues many game devs and more of an art design issue.

If one wants to learn more about the subject\^\[1\], I would recommend reading articles, books and studies on colour theory, composition, visual perception, and graphic design/UX.

\---

\^\[1\]: (which will be a plot and help one to learn on identifying what's good or bad, and the vocabulary and theory)
